title: Trump Has Tried to Exert More Control Over Elections. Here Are the Key Findings From Our Reporting.
content:
Ahead of next week’s midterm elections, President Donald Trump has
[systematically demolished](https://www.propublica.org/article/trump-midterm-
elections-takeover) institutional guardrails that prevented him from
overturning the 2020 presidential election, ProPublica’s reporting has shown.

Trump has empowered [his loyalists](https://www.propublica.org/article/cleta-
mitchell-elections-trump) to try to transform the voting process. He launched
an unprecedented — and largely unsuccessful — effort to find [noncitizen
voters](https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-homeland-
security-investigations). And he tried to [restrict mail-in
voting](https://www.propublica.org/article/trumps-plan-to-restrict-mail-
voting).

Our reporters have spent much of this year covering Trump’s efforts to exert
more federal control over elections. Here are five takeaways from their
reporting.

### 1\. The Trump administration has sought greater federal control over
elections.

In April, Doug Bock Clark and Jen Fifield reported on Trump’s efforts to
“[take over](https://www.propublica.org/article/trump-midterm-elections-
takeover)” the midterm elections, detailing how the administration has
discarded or diminished endeavors across the federal government to protect the
voting process or block foreign interference. Those efforts have included
cutting staff on election-related teams at federal law enforcement agencies
and finding ways to exert greater federal control over voting.

[Our reporting](https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-
homeland-security-investigations) led by Peter Elkind revealed that the Trump
administration harnessed Homeland Security Investigations’ personnel,
technology and legal authority to try to back up Trump’s unproven claim that
illegal voting by noncitizens is tilting elections toward Democrats.
Administration officials insisted the effort spearheaded by HSI was producing
meaningful results. Our analysis of Justice Department data found, as of May,
41 alleged noncitizens were charged with voting illegally or other election-
related crimes. Earlier this month, [CBS
reported](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/federal-agents-seek-noncitizen-voters/)
156 people have been charged since the beginning of the second Trump
administration.

### “Paper Trail” Podcast

Learn more about this story on ProPublica’s podcast “[Paper
Trail](https://www.propublica.org/series/paper-trail).”

As part of that effort, the Justice Department has demanded states turn over
unredacted voter rolls, which contain confidential information on millions of
Americans and have historically been managed by states. Since September 2025,
the department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for the
confidential data. Wary of federal overreach, state officials — including some
Republicans — have [fought back](https://www.propublica.org/article/idaho-
voter-data-trump-justice-department), and so far every DOJ lawsuit that’s been
decided by a federal judge has [been
dismissed](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-doj-voter-data-lawsuits/).
(The Trump administration has appealed most of its losses to federal appeals
courts and has said it will consider taking its fight to the Supreme Court. A
Justice Department spokesperson said its “attorneys are skilled, principled
advocates who argue every case honestly and in good faith.”)

In a March executive order, Trump instructed the U.S. Postal Service to
[create new regulations for mail
voting](https://www.propublica.org/article/mail-voting-usps-officials-
concerns-disenfranchisement). The rules would have put the Postal Service in
the unprecedented role of deciding whether to send or deny the delivery of
voters’ mail-in ballots. The [Supreme Court in September
blocked](https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/09/supreme-court-denies-trump-
administrations-request-to-implement-parts-of-usps-rule-on-mail-in-vo/) the
rules, at least until after November.

The Trump administration has said its actions will make U.S. elections fairer
and more secure — and keep those prohibited from voting, such as noncitizens,
from doing so. Spokespeople for the DOJ and Department of Homeland Security
emphasized that their departments are focused on ensuring elections are free
and fair, and that they are working closely with the states to achieve those
goals. Contentions to the contrary, they say, are false.

### 2\. Trump has pushed out career officials — and is coordinating with a
conservative grassroots organization to transform elections.

At least 75 nonpartisan career officials who’d held roles at federal agencies
related to election integrity and safety have been fired or left the
government.

Two dozen Trump appointees — including many from the election-denial movement
— have been hired. Ahead of the midterms, current and former government
officials and election security experts have expressed concerns that once-
fringe actors who’ve espoused debunked conspiracy theories about elections are
now in positions to control the narrative around the voting process. (A DHS
spokesperson said it hires “experts with diverse backgrounds who go through a
rigorous vetting process.”)

At least 25 administration appointees have close ties to Cleta Mitchell, a
lawyer who leads Election Integrity Network, a grassroots conservative group
focused on transforming America’s voting system. This month, [Clark profiled
Mitchell](https://www.propublica.org/article/cleta-mitchell-elections-trump) —
and detailed how, despite not holding a formal role in the White House, she’s
played a key role in shaping the Trump administration’s elections agenda. The
White House has appointed her associates to help hunt for noncitizen voters
and investigate accusations of voting fraud in 2020. (Mitchell declined
multiple requests to speak with ProPublica, but wrote in an email: “You’re my
opponent. … You’re never going to write in any objective, non-judgmental way
about the election integrity movement.”)

* * *

### Help Us Report on Key Election Issues

ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what
isn’t. We’re monitoring **voter suppression** and interference, **election
observers** and**** poll watchers, **extremism** tied to the election,
and**ICE activity** at the polls. Have you seen something?

[Send Us a Tip](https://www.propublica.org/tips/)

* * *

Mitchell, who played a role in helping Trump challenge his loss in the 2020
presidential election, has been leading efforts to pass state and federal
iterations of the SAVE Act. The 2026 version of the bill, known as the SAVE
America Act, would require voters nationwide to provide proof of citizenship
to register and present a photo ID to vote, and would compel states to turn
over their voter rolls to DHS. Trump has repeatedly called the measure his top
legislative priority, but it has been blocked in the Senate.

In July, Trump also [pushed out](https://www.propublica.org/article/federal-
election-assistance-commission-trump-dismantled) the remaining members of the
bipartisan Election Assistance Commission, a four-member board designed to be
evenly split between Republicans and Democrats that sets standards for state
voting systems. (At the time, a White House official wouldn’t confirm the
moves but said the president “reserves the right to remove individuals that
may not be totally aligned with the important task of securing America’s
elections and ensuring every legal vote is counted.”)

### 3\. Trump officials asked a cybersecurity agency to secretly acquire a
voting machine — and hack it.

A few months into Trump’s second term, political appointees at DHS asked its
Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure a voting machine,
hack it and report the findings so they could be given to the White House, two
former administration officials with knowledge of the request [told Clark and
Andy Mannix](https://www.propublica.org/article/cisa-election-security-donald-
trump).

CISA employees told the political appointees their request was impossible, in
part because the agents capable of pulling off such an operation had just been
laid off by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency. (One of Trump’s
first actions when he returned to the White House was to dismantle the
agency’s election security work.)

Though not acted on, the request shows how the Trump administration has tried
to use the agency for its own ends while draining it of resources for one of
its critical missions: protecting the nation’s voting systems. Since CISA
became an agency in 2018, it has come to provide crucial support to thousands
of local election officials grappling with increasingly sophisticated attacks.

But some state election officials said CISA provided them with little help as
they planned for the 2026 midterms. And other state authorities told Clark and
Mannix that they no longer trusted the agency and feared it had been
compromised by the Trump administration. (A DHS spokesperson told us in April
the “claim that DHS has a broken partnership with states and made our
elections less secure is simply false.”)

DHS did not respond to questions for our October investigation, but a DHS
spokesperson previously told ProPublica that the changes at CISA were in
response to “a ballooning budget concealing a dangerous departure from its
statutory mission,” which included “electioneering instead of defending
America’s critical infrastructure.” A White House spokesperson declined an
interview request but said, “President Trump has done more than any other
President to ensure we have free and fair elections.”

### 4\. The White House floated an idea that would’ve shut down virtually all
mail-in voting.

The White House [initially
proposed](https://www.propublica.org/article/trumps-plan-to-restrict-mail-
voting) a change for the Postal Service that would’ve been even more
disruptive than the rule the Supreme Court rejected in September.

As Fifield and Elkind reported, the Trump administration suggested all ballots
be delivered through certified mail, meaning voters would need to be home to
sign for delivery of their ballots. The Trump administration dropped this plan
after the USPS said it would be too difficult to execute. It instead proceeded
with the [executive order](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-
actions/2026/03/ensuring-citizenship-verification-and-integrity-in-federal-
elections/) that would’ve forced postal workers to serve as gatekeepers,
deciding which ballots would be delivered and which wouldn’t.

In an emailed statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis denied the
administration had interfered improperly with the Postal Service, an
[independent agency](https://about.usps.com/who/government-
relations/assets/establishment-as-independent-agency.pdf) whose governance
structure is specifically designed to protect it from political influence.

The Supreme Court’s order in September means that [voting by mail can proceed
as planned](https://www.propublica.org/article/mail-in-voting-rules-midterm-
elections) for the midterms, with states left to decide the rules for mail-in
ballots.

### 5\. The Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have led to delays and more
rejected ballots in rural areas.

Amid the increased attention on the Postal Service’s role in elections, [a
ProPublica analysis found](https://www.propublica.org/article/mail-ballot-
delays-postal-service-midterms) that delays resulting from the agency’s cost-
cutting measures in recent years have endangered the validity of ballots cast
in rural areas.

The Postal Service has consolidated processing of first-class mail into
regional hubs, and the agency cut the frequency of mail pickups in half at
many post offices 50 miles or more from those processing plants. The changes
often added a day or more to delivery time and pushed back postmarking, an
official mark confirming an envelope has been received by the Postal Service.

Across five states where the best data was available — Washington, California,
Ohio, North Carolina and Oregon — the delays during this year’s primary
elections have had the most substantial effect in areas that voted for Trump
in 2024.

Postal Service leaders say such delays are less likely in the Nov. 3 general
election because of “extraordinary measures” the agency puts in place for
these votes, when there’s typically far more turnout.

Key Findings From Our Reporting.](https://www.propublica.org/article/midterm-
election-propublica-reporting-findings) appeared first on
